hints: Recall whether $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is much more soluble, to state how solubility changes from Mg to Ba.
Think of dissolving as two energy steps, breaking the lattice apart and then hydrating the gaseous ions with water.
Consider how increasing $\text{M}^{2+}$ ionic radius down the group affects attraction to $\text{OH}^{-}$ in the lattice compared with attraction to water molecules.
Decide which enthalpy term falls more quickly when the anion $\text{OH}^{-}$ is small, and what this means for the overall $\Delta H_{sol}$.
walkthrough:
Picture what solubility means here**
Think of adding the solids to water. $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is almost insoluble, it gives only a faintly alkaline solution, while $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is sparingly soluble and $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ and $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ are distinctly more soluble. So solubility increases going down from Mg to Ba.

Split dissolving into two energy changes**
Imagine dissolving $\text{M(OH)}_2(s)$ in two stages. First you pull the lattice apart into gaseous ions, which costs energy equal to $-\Delta H_{latt}$. Then you surround $\text{M}^{2+}(g)$ and $2\text{OH}^{-}(g)$ with water, which releases energy, $\Delta H_{hyd}$. The sum is the enthalpy of solution: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$$ A more exothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$ makes dissolving more favourable.

See why both terms get less exothermic**
Going down the group $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, the cation gets larger so charge density falls. Attraction between $\text{M}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ in the lattice weakens, so $\Delta H_{latt}$ becomes less negative. Attraction between $\text{M}^{2+}$ and water molecules also weakens, so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ of the cation also becomes less negative.

Work out which effect wins for a small anion**
Here the anion $\text{OH}^{-}$ is small while the cation size changes a lot. The lattice energy depends on both $\text{M}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$ radii, so increasing the cation radius has a large proportional effect on the interionic distance. Hydration of $\text{OH}^{-}$ hardly changes, and even cation hydration changes less steeply than the lattice term. So $\Delta H_{latt}$ falls in magnitude faster than $\Delta H_{hyd}$.

Link back to more exothermic solution enthalpy**
Because you pay much less energy to break the lattice but you lose only a little hydration energy, the balance shifts. $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes more negative down the group, so dissolving becomes energetically more favourable and solubility increases.

Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group.
Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic / less negative down the group.
$\Delta H_{latt}$ decreases more rapidly than $\Delta H_{hyd}$ because $\text{OH}^{-}$ is small compared to $\text{M}^{2+}$.
Therefore $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes more exothermic / more negative down the group, favouring dissolving.

hints: Compare the ionic radii and charge densities of $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sr}^{2+}$, both $2+$ ions but from different periods.
Think how a very small, highly charging cation distorts the electron cloud of the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion and weakens bonds within it, making it easier to form $\text{O}^{2-}$.
walkthrough:
Compare the two cations side by side**
Both cations carry the same $2+$ charge, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is much smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ because Mg is in Period 3 and Sr is in Period 5. Same charge packed into a smaller volume means $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has a far higher charge density and therefore a stronger polarising power.

See what strong polarisation does to hydroxide**
Picture $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulling hard on the electron cloud of the neighbouring $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion: $$\text{M(OH)}_2(s) \rightarrow \text{MO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$ This distortion weakens the O-H bond within hydroxide and helps develop the $\text{O}^{2-}$ ion found in the oxide product. The more polarised hydroxide breaks apart with less heating, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ decomposes at a lower temperature than $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$.

Final answer: $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ decomposes at the lower temperature.
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ / has higher charge density, so polarises / distorts the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ion more, weakening it and allowing decomposition to $\text{MgO}$ more easily.
